model_popularity: Everyone gets the same list, the most-interacted items. Test Recall@10 is 0.0249, about 64 times chance (0.0004), and NDCG@10 is 0.0126. For ratings, the shrunk item mean (m = 10, chosen on validation) gives test RMSE 1.2500 against 1.2949 for predicting the global mean.
model_knn: Validation NDCG@10 rises with the number of neighbours kept per item, from 0.0330 at k = 20 to 0.0379 at k = 3200, and is flat from k = 1600 (0.0377), so the winner is not far from the plateau. The final run has test Recall@10 0.0562 and NDCG@10 0.0312, fits in 0.3 s and scores a user in 0.048 ms. It stores 7.1 million similarities.
model_als: Validation NDCG@10 by number of factors: 0.0400 at 32, 0.0449 at 64, 0.0494 at 128, 0.0524 at 256; fit times 16 s, 45 s, 134 s, 796 s. Doubling the factors costs about 5.9 times the training time for a smaller gain each time. Regularisation between 0.01 and 100 barely matters (validation NDCG@10 within 0.0006) and 1000 hurts (0.0210); confidence alpha = 10 is worse (0.0458) and 100 is no better than 40 (0.0493). The final run (256 factors) has test Recall@10 0.0598 and NDCG@10 0.0324. Its validation NDCG@10 (0.0524) is far above its test NDCG@10 because the learned user vectors never saw the validation purchase, which the test item is scored after. Computing each user's vector from the history the harness gives it (the same item factors, nothing retrained; the row called als+history) raises test NDCG@10 from 0.0324 to 0.0432 and Recall@10 from 0.0598 to 0.0785, closing 54% of the validation-to-test gap, so a large part of that gap is the evaluation protocol and not the model. This variant was added after noticing the gap, it has no tunable parameters, and it is reported next to plain ALS, not instead of it.
model_svd: Validation RMSE falls from 1.1538 at reg 0.05 to 1.0968 at reg 0.5 and rises again beyond it; the number of factors hardly matters at that regularisation. Final test RMSE is 1.1785 (MAE 0.8334) against 1.2500 for the popularity baseline, an improvement of 5.7%. As a recommender it is no better than chance: Recall@10 is 0.0003 against 0.0004 for chance. Predicting a rating accurately and ranking the items a user will buy are different problems, and a model trained on rating error does not solve the second.
model_bpr: BPR is sensitive to regularisation. With reg of 0.001 or less, training stopped at the popularity solution (validation NDCG@10 0.0169 against popularity's 0.0136); reg 0.003 to 0.01 learned real preferences (0.0309 and 0.0305); longer patience and 128 factors raised it to 0.0398. The final run has test Recall@10 0.0520 and NDCG@10 0.0271 after 76 of 80 epochs, fitting in 174 s. Its best epoch is at the 80-epoch cap, so it was still improving; a 150-epoch run with weaker regularisation reached the same validation score (0.0398), so BPR looks close to its ceiling on this data but may be slightly undertrained.
model_ncf: The unregularised network memorises the training data: over 10 epochs its training loss fell from 0.41 to 0.06 while validation NDCG@10 stayed near 0.0169 and test Recall@10 was only 0.0250. An L2 penalty on the embeddings and dropout in the MLP helped substantially, though it stays well below the matrix-factorization models: the best setting (reg 0.003, dropout 0.2) reaches test Recall@10 0.0377 and NDCG@10 0.0197. Scoring all items takes 0.62 ms per user, about 13 times KNN, because every user-item pair goes through the MLP; the network has 7.7 million parameters.
model_sasrec: On this small dataset fewer blocks were better at equal dropout 0.2 (validation NDCG@10 0.0327 with one block, 0.0320 with two, 0.0284 with three) and more dropout helped (two blocks: 0.0297 with dropout 0.1, 0.0320 with 0.2, 0.0341 with 0.4). The final model (one block, hidden size 128, dropout 0.5, last 20 purchases) has test Recall@10 0.0632 and NDCG@10 0.0335. Its validation and test NDCG@10 (0.0366 and 0.0335) are close, consistent with it reading the history it is given, which at test time includes the validation purchase. Fit 99 s, scoring 0.016 ms per user, 3.4 million parameters.
model_content: Text similarity alone (lam = 0) reaches test Recall@10 0.0183, 73% of popularity's, with no interaction data about the items. Adding a popularity prior helps up to lam = 0.5 (validation NDCG@10 0.0225); beyond that the model drifts back toward plain popularity. The final run has test Recall@10 0.0382 and NDCG@10 0.0199. The encoder is frozen, so nothing is trained and the run takes 0.01 s once the embeddings are cached.
results_intro: Ranked by test NDCG@10: als+history 0.0432 > sasrec 0.0335 > als 0.0324 > knn 0.0312 > bpr 0.0271 > content 0.0199 > ncf 0.0197 > popularity 0.0126 > svd 0.0002. als+history is first with Recall@10 0.0785 [0.0768, 0.0802] and MRR 0.0385 [0.0376, 0.0395], 3.1 times the popularity baseline (0.0249 [0.0240, 0.0259]) and 201 times chance. Brackets are 95% bootstrap intervals over users; they measure uncertainty from the sample of users, not from training randomness (each model was trained once).
results_significance: als+history is significantly above sasrec (NDCG@10 difference 0.0097, paired bootstrap p < 0.001). als+history is significantly ahead of every other model on NDCG@10; among the models that do not use the history fold-in, sasrec is not significantly above als (NDCG@10 difference 0.0011, paired bootstrap p = 0.057); als is significantly above knn (NDCG@10 difference 0.0013, paired bootstrap p = 0.003). Pairs the data cannot separate (paired p of 0.05 or more): sasrec and als (p = 0.057) and content and ncf (p = 0.712). sasrec is significantly above popularity (NDCG@10 difference 0.0210, paired bootstrap p < 0.001). The weakest personalised models are still clearly above popularity: bpr (0.0271), content (0.0199) and ncf (0.0197).
results_tradeoffs: Cost: training times range from 0.0 s (popularity) to 796 s (als), and scoring from 0.007 ms per user (als) to 0.62 ms (ncf). als+history reaches the top accuracy with a 796 s fit and 0.323 ms per user. ncf needs 83 times the scoring time of als and 1.9 times that of als+history for a much lower NDCG@10 (0.0197 against 0.0432). Personalization versus popularity: popularity recommends the same few items to everyone (coverage@10 0.0008, Gini 0.9996, average training popularity of recommended items 1483), while als+history covers 0.258 of the catalog (Gini 0.941, average popularity 286). The most diverse model is knn (coverage@10 0.965); the models are not equally good at accuracy and diversity, so accuracy alone would hide the popularity trade-off.
results_rating: Only popularity (shrunk item mean) and SVD predict ratings. SVD has the lower test RMSE, 1.1785 against 1.2500 (validation 1.0968 against 1.1795). For scale, predicting the global mean gives 1.2949. The held-out test ratings are more spread out than the training ratings (standard deviation 1.29 against 1.17).
slices: 63.4% of test purchases are of head items (the top 20% by training popularity), 18.3% mid, 17.9% tail and 0.4% items never seen in training. Popularity can only score on head items (Recall@10 0.0393 there, 0.0000 on mid and 0.0000 on tail items). The best model on tail items is knn (Recall@10 0.0230). Models with essentially no skill on tail items: popularity, als, als+history, ncf and sasrec. By user activity (second chart) the cold, warm and heavy thirds are shown for every model.
cold_items: The 345 test purchases of items that never appeared in training: no model has any of them in its top 10. A model that reads item text can in principle reach them. Where the held-out items actually rank (median rank, share in the top 100 and in the top 1,000): popularity: median rank 25,606 of 25,612, 0.0% in the top 100, 0.0% in the top 1,000; knn: median rank 25,606 of 25,612, 0.0% in the top 100, 0.0% in the top 1,000; sasrec: median rank 25,554 of 25,612, 0.0% in the top 100, 0.0% in the top 1,000; content: median rank 16,832 of 25,612, 0.0% in the top 100, 1.4% in the top 1,000. These items have no popularity prior and no neighbours, so they rarely outrank items with any interaction history.
cold_users: New users are 9,476 users held out of training entirely; the model sees only their first n purchases and must rank their last purchase. Recall@10 for n = 0, 1, 2, 3: popularity is flat at 0.0244, the floor (n = 0 means no information, so every model falls back to popularity). knn 0.0244 / 0.0139 / 0.0222 / 0.0278 (passes the floor at n = 3); als 0.0244 / 0.0244 / 0.0244 / 0.0244 (never above the floor); svd 0.0244 / 0.0244 / 0.0244 / 0.0244 (never above the floor); bpr 0.0244 / 0.0244 / 0.0244 / 0.0244 (never above the floor); ncf 0.0244 / 0.0244 / 0.0244 / 0.0244 (never above the floor); sasrec 0.0244 / 0.0223 / 0.0290 / 0.0371 (passes the floor at n = 2); content 0.0244 / 0.0203 / 0.0272 / 0.0317 (passes the floor at n = 2). als, svd, bpr and ncf stay exactly on the floor because they learn a vector per user during training and have none for a new user; they cannot use the revealed purchases. Folding the revealed purchases into ALS with the item factors fixed lifts it to 0.0244 / 0.0309 / 0.0411 / 0.0504. With a single purchase, knn, sasrec and content score below the floor, so they do worse than showing best-sellers. With three purchases the best model is als with fold-in (0.0504, 2.1 times the floor). For comparison, the other 90% of users, with their full history, get Recall@10 0.0595 from sasrec on this data. Revealed purchases help only the models that can use them.
complexity: The proposal asks whether neural and transformer recommenders justify their cost over classical matrix factorization at this data scale. NeuMF's NDCG@10 (0.0197) is significantly below ALS (0.0324) and significantly below BPR (0.0271), and it needs 83 times ALS's scoring time. SASRec's (0.0335) is not significantly different from ALS; als+history is significantly above sasrec (NDCG@10 difference 0.0097, paired bootstrap p < 0.001). SASRec fits in 99 s against 796 s for ALS, has 3.4 million parameters against 30.8 million, and scores at 0.016 ms per user (ALS: 0.007 ms as trained, 0.323 ms when every user is scored from their history). Tuning effort was of the same order for all of them (runs: ncf 12, sasrec 19, als 13, bpr 17, knn 9), but each model was trained once, so differences the paired bootstrap cannot separate should not be read as an ordering. **Answer: neither neural model is significantly better than the best classical model (als, 0.0324), so on this data the extra complexity did not buy accuracy; the most accurate model overall is als+history, a classical matrix factorization.**
popularity_expectation: The proposal also anticipated that the popularity baseline would be surprisingly competitive on raw accuracy while performing poorly on coverage and long-tail items. The coverage and long-tail half held: popularity covers 0.0008 of the catalog at 10, and its Recall@10 is 0.0393 on head items but 0.0000 on mid and 0.0000 on tail items. The accuracy half held only in part: popularity's Recall@10 (0.0249) is far below the leaders (als+history reaches 3.1 times as much, sasrec 2.5 times), so it is not competitive with them, though ncf and content are less than twice as accurate as it (ncf 1.5 times, content 1.5 times), so for the weaker personalised models the baseline is a hard bar to clear.
demo_intro: The recommender in use. We use als+history, the most accurate model with a saved copy (test NDCG@10 0.0432). Given a user it returns ten products; it sees everything known about the user except their held-out last purchase, and never recommends something they already own. Below: a user whose real next purchase is in the top ten, and one where the model misses, shown with titles.
demo_code:
import importlib
from recsys.demo import demo
from recsys.models.base import Recommender

BASE_MODEL = "als"
saved = RESULTS_DIR / "models" / "als_demo.pkl"
if saved.exists():
    model = Recommender.load(saved)
else:   # no saved copy next to the notebook: refit it (minutes)
    module = importlib.import_module(f"recsys.models.{BASE_MODEL}")
    cls = next(c for _, c in vars(module).items() if isinstance(c, type) and issubclass(c, Recommender) and c is not Recommender and c.__module__ == module.__name__)
    model = cls(**FINAL_CONFIGS[BASE_MODEL]); model.fit(data)
    if "+history" in "als+history":
        model.foldin_all = True   # score every user from the history they are given

ranks = np.load(RESULTS_DIR / "per_user" / "als_foldall.npz")["rank_test"]
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
long_history = np.flatnonzero(users["n_train"].to_numpy() >= 8)
hit = int(rng.choice(long_history[ranks[long_history] <= 10]))
miss = int(rng.choice(long_history[ranks[long_history] > 1000]))
print("=== a user whose next purchase the model finds ==="); demo(model, data, hit)

limitations:
- **Single run per model.** Each final model was trained once with one seed. The intervals above come from resampling users, not from retraining; training on the Apple GPU (MPS) is not guaranteed to be bit-for-bit reproducible, and we did not repeat runs with other seeds.
- **Unequal tuning effort.** Runs per model: popularity 1, knn 9, als 13, svd 24, bpr 17, ncf 12, sasrec 19, content 13. Every choice used the validation split only; the test split was used once per model for reporting. The sweep timings were measured while other jobs shared the machine; the final-run timings in the cost table were measured alone.
- **The test protocol favours models that read the history.** The test item is scored after the validation purchase. KNN, SASRec and the content model read it from the history they are given; models with a learned vector per user (ALS, BPR, NeuMF, SVD) do not. Validation minus test NDCG@10: popularity +0.0010, knn +0.0067, als +0.0200, bpr +0.0128, ncf +0.0052, sasrec +0.0030, content +0.0026. The als+history row separates this effect from model quality for ALS. It was added after seeing the gap (not pre-specified); BPR, NeuMF and SVD have no cheap equivalent, so their test numbers are, to the same degree, understated relative to history-based models.
- **Per-user time split.** Each user's last two interactions are held out, rather than one global cut-off date, so a test event can pre-date other users' training events. This is the protocol in the approved proposal.
- **Dense core only.** The 5-core filter keeps 17.9% of interactions and 3.4% of users, so the results describe users with at least five reviews, not typical Amazon shoppers.
- **Cold-start users are simulated.** New users are users held out of training, and the target is their last purchase, which can be many purchases after the revealed ones; a real session would predict the next item.
- **One dataset.** A single Amazon category; ratings are 64% five-star, so rating signals are weak, and results may differ on other domains.
